newsitem.title: INDIA: Spotlight on India Reliance on bonus eve.
newsitem.headline: Spotlight on India Reliance on bonus eve.

text.p: Petrochemicals giant Reliance Industries is expected to announce on Thursday a bonus share issue and possibly tip a rise in sales and profit for the current financial year, analysts said.

"All the good news will come tomorrow," said an analyst at a leading U.S. investment bank. "We expect Reliance to announce a generous bonus ratio and talk about a jump in sales and profit in the current financial year."
Reliance, which began as a commodities trading firm in 1958 and built itself into India's largest private company, was in the market limelight on Wednesday on the eve of the bonus issue.
Reliance said in April its net profit climbed to 13.23 billion rupees ($370 million) in 1996/97 (April-March) from 13.05 billion in the previous year.
Analysts said massive capacity additions commissioned in 1996/97 would drive sales growth in the current year.
"We expect a full year's benefits of these capacities to increase sales volumes by 134 percent in fiscal 1997/98," Goldman Sachs/Kotak Securities said in a recent report.
Chairman Dhirubhai Ambani is due to address shareholders at the firm's annual meeting just after the board of directors meets to finalise the bonus issue.

Rumours of a Reliance bonus issue have grown since the firm's last annual meeting in July 1996 when Ambani told shareholders -- who asked him about a bonus issue -- they would have no cause to complain at the next meeting.
Reliance shares have surged nearly 85 percent since the beginning of this calendar year -- outperforming Bombay's benchmark stock index which has risen just 34 percent in the same period.
"There have been fund managers who ignored the share and because it is such a heavyweight they have underperformed miserably," the analyst at the U.S. firm said.
The rally in Reliance took a breather on Wednesday. The group's shares slipped 2.0 rupees to 372.50 in afternoon trade on the Bombay Stock Exchange.
Traders said they expected the company to announce a bonus ratio of three shares for every five shares held -- the same ratio as the firm's last two bonus issues in the 1980s.
But some traders and analysts forecast that the firm could announce a bonus of one share for every one held.
Another possibility was that Reliance could announce a cash bonus, which, like a dividend payout, would give investors a specific amount of money for every share held.
Reliance Textiles, as it was then called, entered the capital market in November 1977 with an initial public offer (IPO) of 28.2 million rupees.
Market analysts and investors say the firm's IPO and its five subsequent attractively priced rights issues pioneered an equity cult in the country.
Under the leadership of the 64-year-old Ambani, Reliance set the trend for Indian firms who wanted to access international debt and equity markets.

"Your company has until now raised $590 million in three international offerings, the largest total by any single company," Reliance said in its annual report for 1993/94, just a couple of years after India began its gradual conversion to a free- market economy.
Offerings in that year included India's first issue of global depositary receipts and the country's first private Euro convertible issue.
In a recent presentation to analysts, Reliance said it had raised $614 million through debt issues in 1996/97. It said it was the first Asian company to issue 50 and 100 year bonds.

"The company is continuing with its drive to expand capacities in its existing businesses to enable it to be a major global player in most of its product groups," DSP Merrill Lynch vice-president Jyotivardhan Jaipuria said in a recent report, advising investors to "accumulate" the stock.
